content.heading: 6.5 Least-Squares Problems
content.paragraph: Inconsistent systems arise often in applications. When a solution is demanded and none exists, the best one can do is to find an $\textbf{x}$ that makes $A\textbf{x}$ as close as possible to $\textbf{b}$.

Think of $A\textbf{x}$ as an approximation to $\textbf{b}$. The smaller the distance between $\textbf{b}$ and $A\textbf{x}$, given by $\parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$, the better the approximation. The general least-squares problem is to find an $\textbf{x}$ that makes $\parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$ as small as possible. The adjective “least-squares” arises from the fact that $\parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$ is the square root of a sum of squares.

content.paragraph: The most important aspect of the least-squares problem is that no matter what $\textbf{x}$ we select, the vector $A\textbf{x}$ will necessarily be in the column space, $\text{Col~}A$. So we seek an $\textbf{x}$ that makes $A\textbf{x}$ the closest point in $\text{Col~}A$ to $\textbf{b}$. See Figure 1. (Of course, if $\textbf{b}$ happens to be in $\text{Col~}A$, then $\textbf{b}$ is $A\textbf{x}$ for some $\textbf{x}$, and such an $\textbf{x}$ is a “least-squares solution.”)

content.paragraph: Suppose $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ satisfies $A\widehat{\textbf{x}} = \widehat{\textbf{b}}$. By the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem in Section 6.3, the projection $\widehat{\textbf{b}}$ has the property that $\textbf{b} - \widehat{\textbf{b}}$ is orthogonal to $\text{Col~}\textit{A}$, so $\textbf{b} - A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ is orthogonal to each column of $A$. note.title: Theorem ﻿13﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿13﻿
note.paragraph: The set of least-squares solutions of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ coincides with the nonempty set of solutions of the normal equations $A^{T} A\textbf{x} = A^{T}{\textbf{b}}$.

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: As shown, the set of least-squares solutions is nonempty and each least-squares solution $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ satisfies the normal equations. Conversely, suppose $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ satisfies $A^{T} A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ $= A^{T}{\textbf{b}}$. Then $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ satisfies (2), which shows that $\textbf{b} - A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ is orthogonal to the rows of $A^{T}$ and hence is orthogonal to the columns of $A$. Since the columns of $A$ span $\text{Col~}A$, the vector $\textbf{b} - A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ is orthogonal to all of $\text{Col~}A$. Hence the equation

is a decomposition of $\textbf{b}$ into the sum of a vector in $\text{Col~}A$ and a vector orthogonal to $\text{Col~}A$. By the uniqueness of the orthogonal decomposition, $A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ must be the orthogonal projection of $\textbf{b}$ onto $\text{Col~}A$. That is, $A\widehat{\textbf{x}} = \widehat{\textbf{b}}$, and $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ is a least-squares solution.

content.paragraph: In some cases, the normal equations for a least-squares problem can be ill-conditioned; that is, small errors in the calculations of the entries of $A^{T} A$ can sometimes cause relatively large errors in the solution $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$. If the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the least-squares solution can often be computed more reliably through a QR factorization of $A$ (described in Section 6.4).1

By Theorem 12, the columns of $Q$ form an orthonormal basis for $\text{Col~}A$. Hence, by Theorem 10, $QQ^{T}\mathbf{b}$ is the orthogonal projection $\widehat{\textbf{b}}$ of $\textbf{b}$ onto $\text{Col~}A$. Then $A\widehat{\textbf{x}} = \widehat{\textbf{b}}$, which shows that $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ is a least-squares solution of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$. The uniqueness of $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ follows from Theorem 14.

statement.paragraph: (T/F) The general least-squares problem is to find an $\textbf{x}$ that makes $A\textbf{x}$ as close as possible to $\textbf{b}$.

(T/F) Any solution of $A^{T}A\textbf{x} = A^{T}\textbf{b}$ is a least-squares solution of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$.
(T/F) If the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, then the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ has exactly one least-squares solution.
(T/F) The least-squares solution of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ is the point in the column space of $A$ closest to $\textbf{b}$.
(T/F) A least-squares solution of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ is a list of weights that, when applied to the columns of $A$, produces the orthogonal projection of $\textbf{b}$ onto $\text{Col~}A$.
